Hi Amelia — thanks for the clear ask and for sending the questionnaire. Short answer up front: for our hosted API we generally recommend Module Two (Controller-to-Processor) with Module Two + Module Three fallback pattern depending on your role and whether you require additional onward-transfer protections. However, the final choice is driven by the data flows in your DPIA and whether you (MedSecure) act as Controller for the data sent to Redwood.

High-level implementation items we can provide for procurement and DPIA:
- A short rationale memo explaining which module(s) map to common deployment patterns (we'll attach)
- A draft clause you can copy into your DPA addendum for either Module Two or Module Four (we can mark the options)
- Evidence bundle: executed SCCs template, execution checklist, and sample registry entries showing region-level routing controls

I'll loop in Neha (privacy counsel) for the legal nuance and Marcus for details on routing/fallback behavior and how that maps to our smart-routing policies. Would you like an annotated copy of your questionnaire returned, or a one-pager plus the evidence bundle?

—Kim

Hi Amelia — thanks for sending the form. A few points from legal/privacy perspective to help your DPO: 

1) Module recommendation logic (summary):
   - If MedSecure is a Controller that sends customer personal data to Redwood (Processor): Module Two (Controller-to-Processor) is the straightforward fit.
   - If there are onward transfers from Redwood to subprocessors in third countries (e.g., US GPUs), we provide contractual safeguards and typically rely on the SCCs in combination with technical measures (encryption in transit/rest, access controls).
   - In situations where MedSecure acts as Controller but requires that onward transfers be governed by a separate Controller-to-Controller mechanism, we can discuss Module One/Three mix — but that's rare for hosted inference.

2) Required evidence for DPIA:
   - Executed SCCs template indicating selected module(s) (signed copy)
   - Data flow map (high level) showing which categories of data are sent to Redwood and whether any subprocessors will receive identifiable data
   - Routing & fallback description (how requests get routed by region and fallback to compatible model variants) — Marcus can add specifics
   - Ops-to-legal checklist (retention, logging, access, encryption)

3) Practical note on implementation steps for your procurement:
   - We can provide a redlined DPA addendum with the appropriate module marked and pre-filled evidence pointers.
   - For speed, suggest Module Two in the DPA and attach optional language for additional controls if you need to limit certain categories of data or require on-prem options.

Please confirm whether you want our privacy team to produce the redline for your legal team or whether procurement should start with our standard DPA + SCCs template.

Thanks,
Neha Kapoor

Amelia — a few operational details to include in the DPIA checklist that help operationalize the SCCs selection: 

- Routing controls: By default, requests from EU/UK tenants are routed to EU-based clusters. If EU capacity is temporarily constrained we have an automatic fallback to nearest compatible region (US/NA) subject to customer-configured routing policy and their contractual choices. We log any fallback events and can provide routing event export for a limited retention window.

- Onward transfers: We only send tokens/outputs to subprocessors (hosting, monitoring) as required for inference. For customers requiring stricter segregation we can enable dedicated capacity or private deployment (VPC) to avoid standard shared-hosted subprocessors.

- Technical controls we can evidence: TLS enforced, in-transit key management, record of subprocessor contracts, and an ops playbook for incident handling.

I'll attach a short checklist you can drop into your DPIA; it maps the technical controls to the contract clause.

—Marcus
